alt: Four approaches on a scale from the words to the purpose: the literal rule (plain meaning, Whiteley v Chappell), the golden rule (literal unless absurd, Adler v George), the mischief rule (Heydon’s Case, Elliott v Grey) and the purposive approach (Quintavalle), which is now dominant.
caption: The further right, the more the judge looks past the words to what Parliament was trying to do.

alt: The golden rule has a narrow approach, choosing between meanings to avoid absurdity, as in R v Allen (“shall marry” meaning a ceremony), and a broad approach, modifying a single meaning to avoid repugnance, as in Re Sigsworth and ex p Smith. In Adler v George “in the vicinity of” was read as “in or in the vicinity of”.
caption: Narrow: pick the sensible meaning. Broad: change the only meaning to avoid a repugnant result.

alt: Heydon’s Case asks four questions: the common law before the Act, the mischief or defect, the remedy Parliament chose, and the true reason for it; the court then interprets the Act to suppress the mischief. In RCN v DHSS nurses’ involvement was lawful because the mischief was backstreet abortions; in Elliott v Grey a car with no battery was “used on a road”.
caption: Find the defect the Act was passed to cure, then read the words to cure it.

alt: The Act in the centre holds the intrinsic aids: long and short titles, preamble, headings, interpretation sections and schedules. Around it are extrinsic aids: dictionaries of the time, earlier Acts, Hansard, Law Commission reports (Black-Clawson), explanatory notes (Westminster v NASS) and treaties. Hansard is limited by Pepper v Hart to ambiguous Acts and clear statements by a minister or promoter.
caption: Intrinsic aids are in the Act; extrinsic aids come from outside it, Hansard only on the Pepper v Hart conditions.

alt: Three rules of language. Ejusdem generis: “house, office, room or other place” covered indoor places only (Powell v Kempton Park). Expressio unius: “lands, houses and coal mines” excluded other mines (R v Inhabitants of Sedgley). Noscitur a sociis: “interest” among annual payments meant annual interest only (IRC v Frere).
caption: The surrounding words limit the meaning of the word in question.

after: ## Impact of EU law and the Human Rights Act 1998
alt: EU law, while the UK was a member, required national law to be read so far as possible to give effect to EU law, encouraging purposive reasoning. Section 3 of the Human Rights Act requires a Convention-compatible reading so far as possible, even without ambiguity; where impossible, higher courts may make a section 4 declaration of incompatibility, but cannot strike the Act down.
caption: Section 3 reaches further than the ordinary rules; section 4 is the fallback, not a strike-down power.

after: ## Worked example: applying the rules to an unseen statute
alt: Four rules applied to Mia riding an electric wheelchair on a footpath under a fictional Act. Literal: “vehicle” could include a wheelchair, so possibly guilty. Ejusdem generis: a mobility aid is not of the same kind as a bicycle or scooter. Golden: convicting her would be absurd. Mischief or purposive: the Act protects pedestrians from cyclists and scooter riders. Most approaches point to not guilty.
caption: Take each rule in turn: state it, apply it, give a result.
